title: Is it always my fault? The illusion of omnipotence
description: This article explores the psychological phenomenon of personalization — the belief that you are the cause of everything happening around you. It examines the mechanisms of this thinking pattern and its negative consequences, such as stress, anxiety, low self-esteem, and relationship issues. It also looks at the roots of this belief, from childhood influences to cultural norms. Finally, it offers recommendations on how to overcome personalization and free yourself from unfounded guilt.

texts: In any situation, no matter the outcome — I am the cause.
I missed my train — it’s because I took too long to get ready. People on the subway are laughing — they must be laughing at me. My partner is in a bad mood — I must have done something wrong.
Sound familiar?
If so, you may be dealing with a belief in your own omnipotence.
We have all experienced personalization to some degree.
<important>It’s a subtle psychological trap that makes you feel like the center of the universe, forcing you to take responsibility for so much of what happens around you.</important>
You feel convinced that people are reacting solely to you, and that their actions, thoughts, and feelings depend entirely on your behavior, even though most of this is actually beyond your control.
As a result, you suffer, judging yourself and carrying a heavy sense of guilt.
Paradoxically, this belief in your own omnipotence actually limits you, plunging you into anxiety and reducing your effectiveness.
How does personalization manifest?
• “It’s all because of me”: You tend to believe that everything happening in your life is a result of your own actions. Whether it’s good or bad, you take full responsibility.
• “It’s all about me”: You are convinced that people are constantly thinking about you, discussing you, or noticing all your mistakes and flaws.
• “It’s my fault”: Guilt becomes a constant companion, regardless of the actual reasons behind events.
For example:

• Imagine you walk into a shop and the cashier is rude to you. Instead of thinking they might be having a bad day or are just an unkind person, you start blaming yourself: “I must have said or done something wrong.”
• An acquaintance you don’t like is invited to a gathering with your friends. You think they did this on purpose to show you that you aren’t wanted and that they don’t want to hang out with you.
• “If she isn’t answering my call, she must be mad at me.”
• Those teenagers are laughing and whispering — they must be talking about me.

<important>With this way of thinking, it doesn’t matter who is actually at fault — the guilt still feels like yours. Where do you think this leads? It leads to stress, apathy, anxiety, self-esteem issues, and even depression.</important>
Why is personalization dangerous?
• Excessive self-criticism: You may lean toward self-criticism and blaming yourself for events that were actually out of your control.
• Stress and anxiety: The constant feeling that everything is your fault causes chronic stress and anxiety.
• Relationship issues: People prone to personalization may misinterpret the behavior of others, leading to resentment and damaged relationships.
• Distorted perception of reality: Like any irrational belief, personalization misleads you, making it hard to assess situations clearly and causing you to overlook objective facts and circumstances.
• Low self-esteem: By constantly blaming yourself for everything, you undermine your own confidence.
• Victim mentality: Some people try to harm themselves, often without being aware of it, by punishing themselves for imagined mistakes. They may even allow others to treat them poorly.
<q author="Vadim Zeland">Guilt inevitably creates a scenario of punishment, often without your conscious awareness</q>
Where does personalization come from?
This type of belief often forms during childhood.
It is well known that children’s thinking is egocentric, meaning a child sincerely believes they are the cause of everything happening around them.
For example, for three- or four-year-olds, it is perfectly normal to believe that the sun rises because they woke up and sets when it is time for them to sleep.
However, many adults still carry elements of egocentric thinking into their daily lives.
Family or social pressure can also lead a person to feel responsible for the well-being of others — for instance, a child who is forced to care for their parents at an early age.
Self-esteem issues can be both a cause and a consequence of such beliefs.

<important>People with low self-esteem are often prone to personalization. They may feel they don’t deserve to be treated well, and therefore attribute negative events to their own actions or flaws.</important>

Past traumatic experiences can also contribute to personalization. In early childhood, there is a high likelihood of developing distorted thinking and the belief that everything happening depends on them.

For example, if a person frequently heard phrases like “it’s all your fault” or “you never do anything right” from their parents, they might carry that “label” for the rest of their lives, attributing all negative events to their own guilt.
In some cultures, it is common to take responsibility for everything happening around you. This can lead people to be prone to personalization, even when they are not at fault for what is happening.
Regardless of how these beliefs were formed, we can change our thinking at any stage of life if we have the motivation.
In the next chapter, as usual, we will look at key recommendations for working with the belief in one’s own omnipotence.
<q author="Mikhail Bulgakov">You cannot blame yourself for everything if you do not consider yourself omnipotent.</q>

exercise.title: Breaking the “It’s all my fault” trap
exercise.description: This article explains what personalization is — the habit of perceiving events as being personally connected to you. You’ll learn why this thinking pattern causes unnecessary guilt and anxiety, and how to step-by-step develop a more helpful perspective. The techniques provided will help you gently separate facts from thoughts, reduce self-criticism, and find more inner peace.

texts: Sometimes people call personalization “grandiosity,” but it’s not about feeling powerful or important.
Personalization is when it feels like everything happening around you is connected to you, even when there is no evidence for it.
Internally, this often feels less like power and more like anxiety — as if everyone is watching, judging, and expecting you to behave perfectly.
<q author="Marcus Aurelius">Everything we hear is an opinion, not a fact. Everything we see is a perspective, not the truth.</q>
To break this pattern, it’s important to learn how to notice the actual causes of events rather than automatically blaming yourself.
When we take responsibility for things beyond our control, we overload ourselves and create a breeding ground for guilt and exhaustion.
• The first step is observation. Notice when the thought “It’s my fault” pops into your head, even when there are few or no facts to support it.
• Ask yourself: “Did I really influence this situation? Or is this just a thought, not a fact?”
• Try considering other explanations for what is happening. For example: “She didn’t say hello. Maybe she’s upset, in a hurry, or lost in thought — it might have nothing to do with me.”
A series of questions can help:
• Should I really be blaming myself?
• Was this within my control?
• What exactly am I responsible for? Where is the boundary of my responsibility?
• What other reasons could have influenced the situation?
Example:
You arrive at work, and a colleague doesn’t say hello. Automatic thought: “I must have done something wrong.”
<q author="Epictetus">People are not disturbed by things, but by the views they take of them.</q>
Now, let’s analyze it:
• She might not have noticed me, been lost in thought, been sleep-deprived, been in a hurry, or been worried about something else.
• I can’t know the exact reason without a direct conversation.
• Even if she is in a bad mood, it could be due to many factors that have nothing to do with me.
• Since there are no facts, there is no basis for guilt.
We can’t control everything. Sometimes the best step is to let go and let things take their course.
A few exercises that may help:
A New Perspective
Imagine a friend is telling you about the same situation. What would you say to them? How would you support them? You can offer that same support to yourself.
The “What if...” Phrase
Complete the thought: “If I were truly responsible for everything, it would mean..."
For example: “...that I can control how others feel,” or “...that I can read minds,” or “...that I am responsible for every event around me.”
<important>By noticing how absurd these fantasies are, it becomes easier to return to a realistic view of the situation.</important>
Over time, these exercises help you gently separate real facts from automatic guilt.
Remember: being mindful of what happens is valuable. But that doesn’t mean you are responsible for everything.
By letting go of personalization, you regain more lightness, space, and inner peace.
